text.en: A user is granted SELECT on a table through one role and denied SELECT on the same table through another role. What is the effective permission?
Denied — DENY takes precedence over GRANT
Granted — GRANT takes precedence
Whichever role was created first wins
An error is raised at login

explanation.en: An explicit DENY from any path overrides GRANTs. Role creation order is irrelevant, and conflicting permissions don't cause login errors.

example.en: GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::Sales TO Analysts; DENY SELECT ON Sales.Payroll TO Contractors; — a user in both can't read Payroll.

text.en: What does REVOKE do?
Removes a previously granted or denied permission entry
Denies the permission permanently
Drops the user
Grants the permission to everyone

explanation.en: REVOKE deletes an existing GRANT or DENY. Afterwards the principal may still have the permission via another path (e.g. a role). It's not equivalent to DENY (b).

example.en: REVOKE SELECT ON dbo.Orders FROM Bob; — Bob can still read if his role has SELECT.

text.en: An App Service needs to connect to Azure SQL Database without any password or secret. What is the recommended approach?
Enable a managed identity on the App Service and create a database user FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER for it
Store a SQL login password in app settings
Use the server admin login
Embed the password in the source code

explanation.en: Managed identity lets the platform obtain Entra tokens; the database maps the identity to a contained user. No secrets to store or rotate. Options b–d all rely on passwords, and c also violates least privilege.

example.en: CREATE USER [orders-app] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER; ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [orders-app];

text.en: Complete the statements creating a passwordless database user for an app's managed identity.

questions.code:
CREATE USER [inventory-api] FROM [BLANK1];
GRANT [BLANK2] ON SCHEMA::Api TO [inventory-api];

text.en: EXTERNAL PROVIDER
LOGIN
CERTIFICATE
EXECUTE
CONTROL
ALTER

explanation.en: FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER creates a contained user mapped to an Entra identity. EXECUTE on the API schema follows least privilege — the app calls procedures. CONTROL/ALTER would let it change or take over objects.

example.en: Connection string: Authentication=Active Directory Managed Identity;

text.en: A procedure dbo.GetOrders (owner dbo) reads dbo.Orders (owner dbo). A user has EXECUTE on the procedure but no SELECT on the table. What happens when they run it?
It succeeds — ownership chaining skips the permission check on dbo.Orders
It fails with SELECT permission denied
It returns zero rows
It prompts for a password

explanation.en: Unbroken ownership chains mean only EXECUTE on the procedure is checked. This is the classic pattern for exposing data only through procedures.

example.en: GRANT EXECUTE ON dbo.GetOrders TO AppRole; — no table grants needed.

text.en: The same procedure now builds its query with dynamic SQL (sp_executesql). The user gets 'SELECT permission denied'. Why?
Dynamic SQL runs as a separate batch, breaking the ownership chain; permissions are checked against the caller
sp_executesql requires sysadmin
Dynamic SQL is not allowed in procedures
The procedure needs to be recompiled

explanation.en: Ownership chaining doesn't extend into dynamic SQL. Fixes: EXECUTE AS on the module or module signing with a certificate. Recompiling (d) changes nothing.

example.en: CREATE PROCEDURE ... WITH EXECUTE AS OWNER — or sign it and grant SELECT to a certificate user.

text.en: For each statement about Microsoft Entra authentication in Azure SQL, answer Yes or No.
You can create a database user for an Entra group.
Entra-only authentication disables SQL logins on the logical server.
Managed identities require you to rotate their passwords every 90 days.
Entra authentication allows MFA and Conditional Access for human users.

explanation.en: Group-based users centralize membership in Entra. Entra-only auth turns off SQL authentication. Managed identities have no passwords to rotate — the platform handles credentials. Human sign-ins benefit from MFA and Conditional Access.

example.en: CREATE USER [SQL-Readers-Group] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;

text.en: Which statement grants SELECT on every current and future table in the Reporting schema to a role?
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::Reporting TO ReportRole;
GRANT SELECT ON Reporting.* TO ReportRole;
GRANT ALL TABLES IN Reporting TO ReportRole;
ALTER ROLE ReportRole ADD SCHEMA Reporting;

explanation.en: Schema-scoped grants use the SCHEMA:: class and cover objects created later. The other forms are not valid T-SQL.

example.en: Combine with a DENY on a specific sensitive object if needed.

text.en: HR may read Name and Department from dbo.Employees but not Salary. What implements this most directly?
GRANT SELECT ON dbo.Employees(Name, Department) TO HR;
GRANT SELECT ON dbo.Employees TO HR; with Salary masked
RLS on Salary
GRANT ALTER ON dbo.Employees TO HR;

explanation.en: Column-level permissions restrict which columns can be selected; SELECT * would then fail for HR. Masking (b) still allows inference through predicates. RLS (c) filters rows, not columns. ALTER (d) is unrelated and dangerous.

example.en: Alternatively expose a view with only the allowed columns.

text.en: In SQL Server Audit, which object defines WHERE audit records are written?
SERVER AUDIT
DATABASE AUDIT SPECIFICATION
SERVER AUDIT SPECIFICATION
Extended Events session

explanation.en: The SERVER AUDIT is the target (file, Application log, Security log; URL for Managed Instance). Specifications define WHICH actions are captured and point to a server audit. Extended Events underpin auditing but aren't the configuration object here.

example.en: CREATE SERVER AUDIT A1 TO FILE (FILEPATH = 'D:\Audit\');

text.en: Order the steps to audit SELECTs on dbo.Payroll in SQL Server.
CREATE SERVER AUDIT with a file target
ALTER SERVER AUDIT ... WITH (STATE = ON)
CREATE DATABASE AUDIT SPECIFICATION ... ADD (SELECT ON dbo.Payroll BY public)
Read events with sys.fn_get_audit_file

explanation.en: Create the target, enable it, define the database audit specification (which references the audit), then read the results. The specification also needs STATE = ON (typically in its CREATE).

example.en: SELECT * FROM sys.fn_get_audit_file('D:\Audit\*.sqlaudit', DEFAULT, DEFAULT);

text.en: Which three are supported destinations for Azure SQL Database auditing? (Select 3)
Azure Storage account
Log Analytics workspace
Event Hubs
A local file on the server's D: drive
Windows Security event log

explanation.en: Azure SQL Database (PaaS) audits to Storage, Log Analytics or Event Hubs. Local files and Windows event logs are SQL Server targets — you have no OS access in Azure SQL Database.

example.en: Log Analytics: query audits with KQL and build alerts; Event Hubs: stream to a SIEM.

text.en: The security team wants to query audit logs with KQL and raise alerts on suspicious activity. Which Azure SQL auditing destination fits best?
Log Analytics workspace
Azure Storage only
Event Hubs only
sys.fn_get_audit_file

explanation.en: Log Analytics supports KQL queries, workbooks and alert rules natively. Storage is cheap long-term retention; Event Hubs streams to external systems; fn_get_audit_file reads file/storage audits but doesn't provide alerting.

example.en: AzureDiagnostics | where Category == 'SQLSecurityAuditEvents' | where action_name_s == 'DATABASE AUTHENTICATION FAILED'

text.en: Why should applications avoid membership in db_owner?
A compromised app (e.g. via SQL injection) could then alter schema, permissions and security policies
db_owner queries run slower
db_owner can't read data
db_owner is deprecated

explanation.en: Least privilege limits the blast radius: an app with db_owner can drop tables, disable RLS and grant itself anything. Performance (b) is unaffected, db_owner can read everything (c), and it isn't deprecated (d).

example.en: Give apps EXECUTE on an API schema or narrow SELECT/INSERT grants instead.

text.en: Match each statement to its effect.
GRANT
DENY
REVOKE
GRANT ... WITH GRANT OPTION
Gives a permission
Explicitly forbids, overriding grants
Removes a previous grant or deny entry
Lets the grantee grant the permission to others

explanation.en: The core DCL verbs. WITH GRANT OPTION delegates the ability to grant — use sparingly, and REVOKE … CASCADE removes downstream grants.

example.en: REVOKE SELECT ON dbo.T FROM Lead CASCADE; — also removes what Lead granted to others.

text.en: A procedure must read a table owned by a different schema owner, and you want to avoid EXECUTE AS impersonation. Which technique grants exactly that extra permission to the procedure?
Module signing: sign the procedure with a certificate, create a user from the certificate, and grant that user SELECT
Grant the caller db_owner
Enable TRUSTWORTHY on the database
Use WITH RECOMPILE

explanation.en: Signing attaches extra permissions to the code, not the caller, and keeps the caller's identity (useful for auditing). db_owner (b) is excessive; TRUSTWORTHY (c) is a broad, risky setting; RECOMPILE (d) is a plan option.

example.en: CREATE CERTIFICATE SignCert …; ADD SIGNATURE TO dbo.GetData BY CERTIFICATE SignCert; CREATE USER SignUser FROM CERTIFICATE SignCert; GRANT SELECT ON Other.T TO SignUser;

text.en: Which function lists the permissions the current user has on an object?
fn_my_permissions
HAS_DBACCESS
sys.dm_exec_sessions
SUSER_SNAME

explanation.en: fn_my_permissions returns effective permissions for a securable. HAS_DBACCESS checks database access; dm_exec_sessions lists sessions; SUSER_SNAME returns the login name.

example.en: SELECT * FROM fn_my_permissions('dbo.Orders', 'OBJECT');

text.en: For each statement about auditing, answer Yes or No.
Auditing prevents unauthorized queries from running.
A database audit specification references a server audit.
Azure SQL auditing can be configured at server level and apply to all databases.

explanation.en: Auditing records activity; it doesn't block it (permissions and RLS do). Database audit specifications write to a server audit. In Azure SQL, server-level auditing covers every database on the logical server (database-level auditing can add more).

example.en: Detection (audit) + prevention (permissions) + integrity (ledger).

text.en: Many apps share one service identity. Auditors need to know which END USER triggered each update. What helps most?
Have the app set the end-user id in SESSION_CONTEXT and capture it (e.g. in audit columns or triggers)
Rely on server_principal_name in audit logs
Turn off auditing
Use NOLOCK

explanation.en: Audit logs show the shared service identity (b), not the human. Passing the user through SESSION_CONTEXT lets the database record who acted. Disabling auditing (c) and NOLOCK (d) are irrelevant.

example.en: EXEC sp_set_session_context N'UserId', @userId, @read_only = 1; then UpdatedBy DEFAULT CAST(SESSION_CONTEXT(N'UserId') AS NVARCHAR(128)).

text.en: What is a contained database user?
A user that authenticates at the database without a server login (e.g. Entra users in Azure SQL)
A user restricted to one table
A user inside a container image
A user with read-only rights

explanation.en: Contained users live entirely in the database, making it portable (geo-replication, moves) without matching logins. They are not limited to one table or to read-only access.

example.en: CREATE USER [app] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER; — contained Entra user.

text.en: Which .NET connection string setting connects with a system-assigned managed identity?
Authentication=Active Directory Managed Identity
Integrated Security=SSPI
User ID=sa;Password=...
TrustServerCertificate=True

explanation.en: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient supports 'Active Directory Managed Identity' (and 'Active Directory Default'). Integrated Security uses Windows auth, sa uses a password, and TrustServerCertificate controls TLS validation (and shouldn't be true in production).

example.en: For a user-assigned identity add User Id=<client-id>.

text.en: Complete the database audit specification capturing schema changes and payroll updates.

questions.code:
CREATE DATABASE AUDIT SPECIFICATION ChangesSpec
FOR [BLANK1] PayrollAudit
    ADD ([BLANK2]),
    ADD (UPDATE ON dbo.Payroll BY public)
WITH (STATE = ON);

text.en: SERVER AUDIT
EVENT SESSION
DATABASE
SCHEMA_OBJECT_CHANGE_GROUP
FAILED_LOGIN_GROUP
BACKUP_RESTORE_GROUP

explanation.en: Specifications are written FOR SERVER AUDIT <name>. SCHEMA_OBJECT_CHANGE_GROUP captures CREATE/ALTER/DROP of schema objects. FAILED_LOGIN_GROUP is a server-level group, and backup/restore isn't what's asked.

example.en: Server-level groups (logins) go in SERVER AUDIT SPECIFICATION; object-level actions in DATABASE AUDIT SPECIFICATION.

text.en: Where should failed login attempts be captured in SQL Server Audit?
A SERVER AUDIT SPECIFICATION with FAILED_LOGIN_GROUP
A DATABASE AUDIT SPECIFICATION on each table
A trigger on sys.logins
The query store

explanation.en: Logins are server-scoped events, so they belong in a server audit specification. Table-level specs (b) can't see logins, system views can't have triggers (c), and Query Store (d) tracks query performance.

example.en: CREATE SERVER AUDIT SPECIFICATION LoginSpec FOR SERVER AUDIT A1 ADD (FAILED_LOGIN_GROUP) WITH (STATE = ON);

text.en: A table-level DENY SELECT exists on dbo.Employees for a user, and a column-level GRANT SELECT on dbo.Employees(Name) is added. Under default settings, can the user SELECT Name?
Yes — a column-level GRANT overrides a table-level DENY (legacy behavior), unless common criteria compliance is enabled
No — DENY always wins in every case
Only if the user is db_owner
The GRANT fails with an error

explanation.en: This is the documented exception to 'DENY wins': column-level GRANT takes precedence over table-level DENY for backward compatibility. Enabling common criteria compliance changes this so the DENY wins.

example.en: Know the rule AND its exception — hard questions target the exception.

text.en: Why grant permissions to roles instead of individual users?
Easier management and review: change membership instead of re-granting many permissions
Roles make queries faster
Users can't receive permissions directly
Roles bypass DENY

explanation.en: Role-based access keeps permission sets consistent and auditable. Users can technically receive direct grants (c), roles don't affect performance (b), and DENY still applies (d).

example.en: With Entra, map an Entra group to a database role for central membership management.

text.en: Which two are benefits of passwordless (managed identity) database access? (Select 2)
No secrets in configuration to leak or rotate
Access can be revoked centrally in Microsoft Entra ID
Grants the app sysadmin automatically
Removes the need for database permissions

explanation.en: Managed identities eliminate stored credentials and centralize identity lifecycle. They grant nothing by themselves (c) — database users and permissions are still required (d).

example.en: Disable the identity or remove its database user to cut access immediately.

text.en: A developer gets 'Login failed for user <token-identified principal>' connecting with a managed identity. What's the most likely cause?
No database user exists for that identity (CREATE USER … FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER was never run)
The password expired
The query is too slow
TDE is enabled

explanation.en: Token authentication succeeds at Entra, but the database needs a user mapped to the identity. Managed identities have no passwords (b); performance (c) and TDE (d) don't cause login failures.

example.en: Also verify the Entra admin is configured on the logical server so FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER works.

text.en: Answer Yes or No for each least-privilege practice.
Use a separate identity for each application.
Let all apps share the server admin login for simplicity.
Expose writes through procedures with EXECUTE grants.
Grant CONTROL on the database to reporting tools.

explanation.en: Separate identities give attribution and isolation; procedure-based access narrows what apps can do. Shared admin logins and CONTROL for reporting tools violate least privilege.

example.en: Reporting: SELECT on a reporting schema or views — never CONTROL.

text.en: Which permission lets a user see execution plans without granting broader rights?
SHOWPLAN
CONTROL
ALTER ANY USER
UNMASK

explanation.en: SHOWPLAN allows viewing plans (still requiring permission on the queried objects). CONTROL is far broader, ALTER ANY USER manages users, and UNMASK reveals masked data.

example.en: GRANT SHOWPLAN TO PerfAnalysts;

text.en: Performance engineers need to query server-level DMVs in Azure SQL without admin rights. Which built-in role helps?
##MS_ServerStateReader## (server role in master)
db_owner
db_datawriter
public

explanation.en: Azure SQL provides granular server roles like ##MS_ServerStateReader## (VIEW SERVER STATE) so you don't hand out admin. db_owner is excessive, db_datawriter is unrelated, public grants almost nothing.

example.en: ALTER SERVER ROLE ##MS_ServerStateReader## ADD MEMBER [perf-team-login];

text.en: Match each scenario to the security feature.
Record who read the Payroll table
Stop contractors reading Payroll
Prove Payroll rows weren't altered by admins
Let the payroll app connect with no password
Auditing
DENY / permissions
Ledger
Managed identity + Entra auth

explanation.en: Detection → auditing; prevention → permissions; integrity proof → ledger; passwordless access → managed identity.

example.en: One table can use all four controls together.

text.en: Why is setting a database TRUSTWORTHY ON considered risky?
Code impersonating principals in that database can gain server-level permissions of the database owner, enabling privilege escalation
It disables backups
It turns off auditing
It encrypts the database

explanation.en: TRUSTWORTHY lets impersonation contexts reach outside the database; if the owner is highly privileged (e.g. sa), a db_owner can escalate to sysadmin. Prefer module signing. It doesn't affect backups, auditing or encryption.

example.en: Microsoft guidance: keep TRUSTWORTHY OFF; use certificate signing for cross-database access.

text.en: Which view shows explicit permissions granted or denied in the current database?
sys.database_permissions
sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
sys.masked_columns
sys.dm_os_wait_stats

explanation.en: sys.database_permissions lists permission entries (state GRANT/DENY, class, grantee). The other views cover indexes, masking and waits.

example.en: Join with sys.database_principals for readable grantee names.

text.en: To give an Entra group read access to a SQL database in Fabric or Azure SQL, the cleanest approach is:
CREATE USER [Group-Name] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER and add it to a role with the needed grants
Create a SQL login per group member
Share one SQL password with the group
Grant the group sysadmin

explanation.en: Group-mapped users let Entra membership control access. Per-member SQL logins (b) and shared passwords (c) defeat central identity; sysadmin (d) is excessive.

example.en: New team member? Add them to the Entra group — no database change needed.

text.en: Answer Yes or No about ownership chains.
A view owned by dbo selecting from a table owned by 'sales' (different owner) breaks the chain.
Cross-database ownership chaining is enabled by default.
Ownership chaining also skips RLS predicates.

explanation.en: Different owners break the chain, so the caller needs permission on the table. Cross-database chaining is off by default (and should usually stay off). RLS predicates are always evaluated; chaining affects only permission checks.

example.en: Keep objects in a schema owned by one principal to keep chains simple.

text.en: What is Microsoft Defender for SQL's role relative to auditing?
It adds threat detection (e.g. SQL injection, anomalous access) and vulnerability assessment on top of logging
It replaces permissions
It encrypts columns
It is the same as auditing

explanation.en: Defender for SQL analyzes activity for threats and flags misconfigurations; auditing provides the raw activity record. It doesn't replace permissions or encrypt data.

example.en: Alerts like 'Potential SQL injection' or 'Login from an unusual location'.

text.en: Complete the role setup for a reporting team.
ROLE
GROUP
LOGIN
ADD MEMBER
INCLUDE
GRANT TO

explanation.en: CREATE ROLE defines a database role; ALTER ROLE … ADD MEMBER adds principals. CREATE GROUP doesn't exist, CREATE LOGIN is server-level, and INCLUDE/GRANT TO aren't ALTER ROLE syntax.

example.en: sp_addrolemember is the deprecated older syntax.

text.en: Azure SQL auditing is enabled at the server level and also at the database level with the same destination. What is the result?
Both policies apply, so events may be recorded twice; server-level alone is usually enough unless the database needs different settings
The database policy disables the server policy
Auditing fails to start
Only failed logins are recorded

explanation.en: Server and database auditing are independent; enabling both can duplicate records. Microsoft recommends server-level auditing unless a database needs additional or different action groups or destinations.

example.en: Use database-level auditing for one database that needs extra retention or a different storage account.

text.en: Which statement explicitly forbids a user from deleting rows in dbo.Orders?
DENY DELETE ON dbo.Orders TO TheUser;
REVOKE INSERT ON dbo.Orders FROM TheUser;
GRANT DELETE ON dbo.Orders TO TheUser;
DROP USER TheUser;

explanation.en: DENY DELETE blocks deletes regardless of grants elsewhere. Revoking INSERT (b) is a different permission, GRANT (c) is the opposite, and dropping the user (d) is not what's asked.

example.en: Use DENY sparingly — it can confuse troubleshooting; prefer not granting in the first place.

text.en: Order the steps to move an app from SQL authentication to managed identity.
Enable a managed identity on the app's hosting resource
Create a database user FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER and grant least-privilege permissions
Change the connection string to Active Directory Managed Identity and deploy
Remove the old SQL login/password (optionally enable Entra-only auth)

explanation.en: Identity first, then database mapping, then app change, then retire the old secret. Removing the SQL login before the app switches would cause an outage.

example.en: Finally consider Entra-only authentication to block SQL logins server-wide.

text.en: Which function reads SQL Server Audit file contents with T-SQL?
sys.fn_get_audit_file
sys.fn_xe_file_target_read_file only
OPENROWSET(BULK ...) with SINGLE_CLOB
DBCC AUDIT

explanation.en: sys.fn_get_audit_file parses .sqlaudit files (also from Azure Storage for Azure SQL). The XE reader is for Extended Events files, OPENROWSET can't parse the binary format, and DBCC AUDIT doesn't exist.

example.en: SELECT event_time, action_id, statement FROM sys.fn_get_audit_file('https://acct.blob.core.windows.net/sqldbauditlogs/...', DEFAULT, DEFAULT);

text.en: Answer Yes or No for each statement about permissions hierarchy.
CONTROL on a schema implies SELECT on its tables.
SELECT granted on a schema applies to tables created in it later.
A permission on a table automatically grants it on other schemas.

explanation.en: Higher permissions imply lower ones (CONTROL ⊃ SELECT), and schema-scoped grants cover future objects. Permissions never spread sideways to other schemas.

example.en: Use the permissions poster/chart to see implication chains.

text.en: An external model is used by AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS. Which permission must an app user have to call it?
EXECUTE on the external model (GRANT EXECUTE ON EXTERNAL MODEL::name)
CONTROL SERVER
ALTER ANY EXTERNAL MODEL
No permission is needed

explanation.en: Using a model requires EXECUTE on it; creating/altering requires CREATE/ALTER ANY EXTERNAL MODEL. CONTROL SERVER is excessive. Permissions are definitely required.

example.en: GRANT EXECUTE ON EXTERNAL MODEL::EmbeddingModel TO [search-api];

text.en: A procedure uses EXECUTE AS OWNER to run privileged cleanup. Auditing shows the owner, not the caller. How can you keep the caller's identity visible?
Use module signing instead of EXECUTE AS, or capture ORIGINAL_LOGIN() inside the procedure
Disable auditing
Use EXECUTE AS CALLER and grant callers sysadmin
It's impossible

explanation.en: Signing adds permissions without changing execution context, so audits show the real caller. ORIGINAL_LOGIN() returns the login that started the session even under impersonation. Granting sysadmin (c) defeats the purpose.

example.en: INSERT INTO dbo.CleanupLog (RunBy) VALUES (ORIGINAL_LOGIN());

text.en: Which authentication method should human DBAs use for Azure SQL to benefit from MFA?
Microsoft Entra authentication (interactive with MFA)
A shared SQL login
The sa account
Anonymous access

explanation.en: Entra interactive authentication supports MFA and Conditional Access. Shared SQL logins and sa provide neither, and anonymous access isn't supported.

example.en: SSMS: Authentication = 'Microsoft Entra MFA'.

text.en: An app identity needs to read data but never change schema. Which fixed database roles are appropriate?
db_datareader (or narrower custom grants)
db_ddladmin
db_owner
db_securityadmin

explanation.en: db_datareader allows SELECT on all user tables. db_ddladmin changes schema, db_owner does everything, db_securityadmin manages permissions. Even narrower custom grants are often better than database-wide read.

example.en: Prefer GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::Api if the app needs only one schema.

text.en: Which two audit configurations best support investigating a suspected data leak from a sensitive table? (Select 2)
Audit SELECT on the sensitive table (database audit specification / action group)
Send audit logs to a destination with alerting and sufficient retention (e.g. Log Analytics)
Audit only failed logins
Store audit files on the same disk as the data with no retention

explanation.en: You need to record reads of the table and keep logs where they can be analyzed and retained. Failed logins alone (c) miss authorized-but-abused access; unretained logs next to the data (d) are fragile and may be tampered with.

example.en: Combine with SESSION_CONTEXT to attribute reads behind service identities.

text.en: In SQL Server 2022+ connected through Azure Arc, what enables Microsoft Entra authentication?
Configuring an Entra admin for the Arc-enabled instance; then CREATE LOGIN/USER FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER
It's impossible on SQL Server
Installing Active Directory Federation Services
Enabling TDE

explanation.en: SQL Server 2022+ supports Entra authentication via Azure Arc with an Entra admin configured. It's not limited to Azure SQL (b); ADFS (c) isn't required; TDE (d) is unrelated.

example.en: The same Arc connection provides the managed identity used for external models in SQL Server 2025.

text.en: Is each item a passwordless approach for application access? Answer Yes or No.
System-assigned managed identity
User-assigned managed identity
SQL login with a 32-character password in Key Vault

explanation.en: Both managed identity types avoid secrets. A SQL login password is still a secret — storing it in Key Vault is better than in config, but it isn't passwordless.

example.en: User-assigned identities can be shared across resources and survive resource recreation.

text.en: Match each permission problem to its best fix.
Procedure with dynamic SQL fails for callers
Dozens of users each have individual grants
App connection string contains a SQL password
DBAs need DMV access but not admin rights (Azure SQL)
Module signing or EXECUTE AS
Roles (mapped to Entra groups)
Managed identity
##MS_ServerStateReader##

explanation.en: Dynamic SQL breaks ownership chains → signing/EXECUTE AS; scattered grants → roles; passwords → managed identity; DMV access → granular server role.

example.en: Least privilege applied to four common situations.
